explanations.explanation: Fulfill, baker. Jesus says, “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them.” I know what it feels like to get shoved in a junk drawer, and that is NOT what Jesus is doing with the Law and the Prophets. He's saying they're not going anywhere.

I get why that one tempts you, friend. But Jesus never says simplify. He says, “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them.” So the Law and the Prophets aren't getting trimmed down to a shorter recipe card.

Soften sounds nice and gentle, but it's not what Jesus says. He says, “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them.” Then in the very next verse He says not a jot or a stroke of a pen will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished. Nothing in there sounds like turning the oven down.

True. Jesus says, “…not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished.” A jot and a stroke are the smallest marks in the writing. If the little marks stay, you know the big words stay too.

This one is true, baker. Jesus says the opposite of that, “…not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished.” Jots and strokes are the tiniest marks in the writing. Even those stay put.

That's it, friend. Jesus says whoever practices and teaches the commandments “…will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” Notice the two parts, doing it and teaching it. I like that He puts them side by side.

explanations.answer: Called a teacher of the Law
explanations.explanation: Close on the teaching part, but that's not the title Jesus gives. He says the one who practices and teaches these commandments “…will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” The word is great, and it goes right across from least. Nobody is handing out a teacher badge here.

explanations.answer: Called a friend of the prophets
explanations.explanation: I'd take that title any day, but Jesus doesn't use it here. He says whoever practices and teaches the commandments “…will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” That's the other side of being called least. Prophets come up in verse 17, but the great-in-the-kingdom line is the one that answers this question.

I know that sounds reasonable, friend, but it's false. Jesus says, “…unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.” Equal isn't enough. The bar is higher than theirs.

False is right. Jesus says, “…unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.” Matching them isn't enough. He says it has to exceed theirs.

Angry, baker. Jesus says, “…anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment.” The old command was about murder, and He takes it down to what's going on inside a person. This is the first time He does that, and the rest of the passage follows the same pattern.

Dishonesty matters, but that's not the word in this verse. Jesus says anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment. He's taking “Do not murder…” and going down to anger. Honesty comes up later in the passage, with oaths.

Stingy is a sneaky pick, friend, since giving comes up near the end of this passage. But here Jesus is on the command about murder. He says anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment. The word is angry.

explanations.answer: Leave the gift and go reconcile first
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jesus says, “…leave your gift there before the altar. First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.” The gift waits and the brother gets the first visit. Picture walking out mid-offering. That takes guts.

explanations.answer: Offer the gift and pray for him after
explanations.explanation: Praying is a good thing, friend, but that's not the order Jesus gives. He says, “…leave your gift there before the altar. First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.” The word is first. The gift comes after the reconciling.

explanations.answer: Bring a bigger gift to make up for it
explanations.explanation: I admit I've tried that with a bigger batch of cookies. Jesus doesn't say anything about a bigger gift, though. He says to leave the gift there, go and be reconciled to your brother first, and then come and offer it.

That's the opposite of what Jesus says, friend, so it's false. He says, “Reconcile quickly with your adversary, while you are still on the way to court.” Waiting around for the judge isn't the advice. Fixing it early is.

False is right. Jesus says, “Reconcile quickly with your adversary, while you are still on the way to court.” The moment to make peace is on the road, before anyone ever reaches the judge. Waiting is the part He warns about in the next lines.
The last penny, baker. Jesus says, “…you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.” He doesn't say close enough or most of it. It's the whole amount, down to the final coin.

Half would be a nice discount, friend, but Jesus doesn't offer one. He says, “…you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.” That's the whole debt, not a part of it. I could use a half-price deal on the flour bill, though.

The judge is in the story, but Jesus names the amount. He says, “…you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.” Jesus says the judge may hand you over to the officer, and you may be thrown into prison. The last penny is what has to be paid.

Heart, baker. Jesus says anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her “…has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” It's the same move as with murder, where He goes from the act to what's inside. This is a serious one, and He means it.

House is a fair guess if you're picturing where this happens, but Jesus says something else. He says the man “…has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” He's talking about what's going on inside a person. The old command stays, and He goes deeper than the act.

Words did matter in the verses on anger, so I see the pull. But here Jesus says the man “…has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” The word is heart. Same pattern as before, just a different command.

explanations.answer: Better to lose one part than your whole body in hell
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Jesus gives. About the eye, He says, “It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell.” About the hand, it's the same idea, with the whole body departing into hell. It's intense language, baker. I think He's showing how serious it is.

explanations.answer: The eye and the hand were counted the most unclean
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says anything about being unclean here. His reason is right in the verse. He says, “It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell.” The weight is on the whole body.

explanations.answer: The priests required it after any sin at all
explanations.explanation: No priests in this part, friend. The reason comes straight from Jesus, who says it is better to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell. He's not describing a rule the priests made. He's the one speaking, and He gives His own reason.

Sexual immorality, baker. Jesus says anyone who divorces his wife, “…except for sexual immorality, brings adultery upon her.” That's the one exception He names. It's a heavy topic, and He's careful with every word.

Her family doesn't come up in this verse, friend. Jesus names one exception, and it's sexual immorality. He says anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, brings adultery upon her. Family consent isn't part of what He says.

The certificate is from what they'd heard in verse 31, so I see why it stuck. But when Jesus gives His own word, the exception is sexual immorality. He says anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, brings adultery upon her. The certificate isn't the exception.
True. After what they'd heard about keeping their oaths, Jesus says, “…I tell you not to swear at all…” That's a big turn, baker. He's going down to the heart of the matter again.
This one is true, friend. The old words were to fulfill your vows to the Lord. Then Jesus says, “…I tell you not to swear at all…” The 'But I tell you' pattern is back.

King, baker. Jesus says Jerusalem is “…the city of the great King.” Look at the list He builds in Matthew 5:34 and 35: heaven is God's throne and the earth is His footstool. Jerusalem is added right after them, with its own reason attached.
A temple is a fair guess, friend, but the verse never mentions one. It says Jerusalem is “…the city of the great King.” The word the verse gives is King.
A council did show up earlier, in the verse about the Sanhedrin. Here, though, Jesus says Jerusalem is “…the city of the great King.” Different verse, different word.

Nope, friend, it's false. Jesus says, “Nor should you swear by your head, for you cannot make a single hair white or black.” He just shut the door on heaven, earth and Jerusalem, and your own head doesn't get a pass. His reason is that you cannot make a single hair white or black.

False is right. Jesus says, “Nor should you swear by your head, for you cannot make a single hair white or black.” Your head isn't an exception. He gives the reason Himself: you cannot make a single hair white or black.

explanations.answer: Let your yes be yes and your no be no
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says, “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’…” No big oath needed, just a plain answer you stand behind. Honestly, that's a lot easier to keep track of.

explanations.answer: Make every promise in front of witnesses
explanations.explanation: Witnesses make sense in a lot of places, but Jesus doesn't ask for them here. He says, “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’…” A plain yes or no is the whole instruction.

explanations.answer: Swear only by the name of the Lord
explanations.explanation: That one sounds holy, friend, but it's not what Jesus says. He said, “…I tell you not to swear at all…” Then He says, “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’…” So He's pointing away from swearing and toward plain words.

True. Jesus says, “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’ Anything more comes from the evil one.” He says it right after telling them not to swear at all. That's a serious thing to say, baker.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says, “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’ Anything more comes from the evil one.” It comes right after He tells them not to swear at all, so the extra is anything beyond a plain Yes or No.

Do not resist him, baker. Jesus says, “…I tell you not to resist an evil person.” They'd heard 'Eye for eye and tooth for tooth,' and He gives them something completely different. That's the same 'You have heard… But I tell you' pattern as the rest of the passage.

That's the old saying, friend, not what Jesus says. They'd heard “Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.” Then He says, “…I tell you not to resist an evil person.” Paying back is the thing He's turning away from.

The judge shows up earlier in the passage, so that pick has some history. But here Jesus says, “…I tell you not to resist an evil person.” He follows it with a slap on the cheek, and what to do about it. Nothing about a judge in this part.
True. Jesus says, “If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also…” That's a hard one, baker. He doesn't say it will be easy. He just says it.
This one is true, friend. Jesus says, “If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also…” I think that goes against how most of us feel. It's still what He says.
Two, baker. Jesus says, “…if someone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles.” Do the first mile, then keep walking. I'd be asking for a rest at mile one and a half.

Three is generous, friend, but Jesus says two. The verse reads, “…if someone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles.” One mile forced, one more freely. I'm relieved it's not three, honestly.
Seven miles! That's ambitious, baker. I'd need a very sturdy gold base for that. But Jesus says, “…if someone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles.” The number is two.

That's half right, friend, so the whole thing comes out false. Jesus says to give to the one who asks, and then, “…do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.” He doesn't split them. Both get an open hand.

False is right. Jesus says, “Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.” The asker and the borrower both get the same open hand. Nobody gets sent to a different line, baker.

explanations.answer: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you…” They'd heard to hate their enemy, and He flips it. Love and prayer for the very people who persecute them.

explanations.answer: Love your neighbor and keep away from your enemies
explanations.explanation: That's a natural middle ground, friend, but it's not what Jesus says. He says, “…love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you…” Keeping distance isn't part of the instruction. Love and prayer are.

explanations.answer: Forgive your enemies once they make things right
explanations.explanation: Forgiveness is a good thing, but this isn't what Jesus says. His words are, “…love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you…” He doesn't add a condition like waiting for them to make things right. The instruction is love and prayer.
Sons, baker. Jesus says to love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, “…that you may be sons of your Father in heaven.” It's about being family. Then He points to how the Father acts.
Servants is a decent guess, friend, but that's not the word. Jesus says, “…that you may be sons of your Father in heaven.” The picture is family, not a job. Same Father, same household.
Guests would be a fine picture, since I do love having guests in my bakery. But the verse says, “…that you may be sons of your Father in heaven.” It's about being sons. That's closer than a guest.
That's not what Jesus says, so it's false. He says the Father “…sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.” Both get rained on, friend, so nobody's getting a private cloud.
False is right. Jesus says the Father “…sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.” It falls on both. Same with the sun, which He causes to rise on the evil and the good.

explanations.answer: It's nothing more than others already do
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus asks, “…what are you doing more than others?” Tax collectors love those who love them, and Gentiles greet their own brothers. So loving only your own isn't going beyond.

explanations.answer: It earns a reward from the Father
explanations.explanation: Jesus actually asks the question the other way around. He says, “If you love those who love you, what reward will you get?” Then He points out that even tax collectors do the same. His point is that it's nothing more than others already do.

explanations.answer: It's the hardest love there is to give
explanations.explanation: Jesus never calls it the hardest, friend. The hard one is loving your enemies, and He's just told them to do that. About loving only your own, He asks, “…what are you doing more than others?” Tax collectors love those who love them, and Gentiles greet their brothers.

Perfect, baker. Jesus says, “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” After all that talk about loving enemies, He points to the Father as the example. It's a big word, and it's the word He uses.

Patience is a good thing, and I need plenty of it with a stubborn dough. But Jesus uses a different word. He says, “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” That's the word He ends on.

Generous fits a lot of what Jesus just said, friend, like giving to the one who asks. But the word He uses to sum it up is a different one. He says, “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”
